title: US Athletic & Sporting Goods Manufacturing: 2025-2026 State of the Industry
one_liner: A $10 billion domestic manufacturing sector supplying roughly half of US sporting goods demand while contending with 34% tariffs on Chinese imports and aggressive supply-chain reshuffling to escape duties.
overview: The US athletic and sporting goods manufacturing industry faces a structural inflection point in 2025-2026. Domestic production sits at $10.0 billion in 2026, down from $10.8 billion in 2024, even as the broader sporting goods market (retail and wholesale combined) reached $130 billion in 2025 wholesale alone. The industry remains heavily dependent on foreign production: China accounts for 61% of the $10.3 billion in annual imports, making tariffs the primary existential concern for manufacturers, brands, and retailers for the first time. Nike, Adidas, and other majors are scrambling to diversify sourcing to India, Indonesia, and Vietnam to hedge against tariffs at 34% for Chinese goods (as of April 2025) and 25% for steel and aluminum. Meanwhile, participation-driven demand (pickleball up 22% year-over-year, golf at 48 million participants, baseball rebounding) is sustaining the wholesale market, but domestic manufacturers are squeezed between tariff costs, price pressure from consumers, and the need to automate or shut down.

key_stats.market_size: $10.0 billion domestic manufacturing (2026); $130 billion broader sporting goods wholesale (2025)
key_stats.growth: -0.13% for manufacturing (2024-2025); 3.7% for broader industry (2025 wholesale YoY); pickleball 22% YoY (2025)
key_stats.businesses: 1,374 establishments in domestic manufacturing (2025)
key_stats.employees: 31,500 workers in domestic manufacturing; average household spending on sports rose 46% since 2019 to $1,016 annually
key_stats.concentration: Low concentration; imports represent roughly 56% of domestic demand; China alone 61% of $10.3 billion annual imports (2024-2025)
key_stats.profit_margin: 6.0% average profit margin (2022 baseline)

one_sentence: The industry is shrinking domestically even as overall sporting goods demand grows, caught between Chinese tariffs at 34%, consumer price resistance, and a supply chain under forced migration to Asia's lower-tariff countries.
current_dynamics: Tariffs have become the dominant force reshaping the industry in real time. In April 2025, the US imposed 34% tariffs on Chinese sporting goods, and separately raised duties on steel and aluminum to 25%. For the first time ever, tariffs surpassed all other concerns (competition, consumer trends, labor costs) to become the top worry across manufacturers, brands, and retailers regardless of size. Domestic manufacturers now face a brutal squeeze: they cannot compete on price with cheap imports; consumers push back on price increases; and brands are moving production to Vietnam, India, and Indonesia to escape tariff exposure. Nike has already raised US prices in June 2025 after failing at a North American reshoring experiment in Mexico. Adidas opened a partial automation plant in Atlanta and announced price hikes. Under Armour and others discuss Baltimore operations, but reshoring remains a niche move at tiny scale compared to overall imports. The broader market is sustained by real participation gains (golf 48 million participants in 2025, pickleball 9.6 million and growing 22% YoY), but domestic manufacturers capture only about half the value as imports flood the channel. Youth sports participation hit a 12-year high in 2024-2025, but family spending pressures (46% increase since 2019) and widening income inequality are starting to throttle access.
how_it_makes_money: Domestic manufacturers make money by selling sporting goods (golf clubs, balls, protective gear, fishing tackle, playground equipment, custom boards) to wholesalers and retailers. Golf equipment alone accounts for 28.5% of domestic revenue. Roughly half of US domestic demand is fulfilled by domestic manufacturers; the other half is supplied by imports (primarily from China at 61%). Manufacturers have begun bypassing wholesalers to sell directly to retailers, which improves margins. High-value custom and niche products (customized golf clubs, stand-up paddleboards, snowshoes) generate better margins than commodity goods. Exports to other countries are minimal at $1.7 billion annually and flat. Most profit comes from differentiation, specialization, and direct-to-retailer channels rather than scale or price competition.
whats_growing: Pickleball equipment sales surged 22% year-over-year in 2025 as the sport reached 9.6 million US participants (22% growth YoY). Golf participation jumped to a record 48.1 million Americans in 2025 (29.1 million on-course, 19 million off-course), with women's golf up 46% since 2019. Baseball and softball grew 7.9% in 2025 after years of decline, boosted by youth sports participation at a 12-year high. Team uniforms surged 5.4% annually and 75.9% since 2020. Athletic footwear, the category leader at $24.1 billion, continues outpacing industry average growth. Institutional fitness equipment (gyms, commercial facilities) is strong, though consumer home fitness gear declined. Overall youth sports participation hit 65% of ages 6-17 in 2024 (up from 59% in 2021). However, these participation gains fuel wholesale demand, not necessarily domestic manufacturing growth because imports capture 56% of that demand.
whats_shrinking: Domestic manufacturing revenue fell 0.13% from 2024 to 2025, while the number of domestic manufacturers has contracted at 1.3% annually since 2005. Golf's share of domestic manufacturing revenue declined from 28.5% in 2022 as golf participation bottomed in the 2010s, though it has since recovered. Department store demand, a traditional buyer of sporting goods, has declined 4.4% annually over the past 17 years. Home fitness equipment sales contracted as pandemic-era at-home workouts faded and consumers returned to gyms. Golf participation among millennials remains low despite overall participation recovery, dragging on that category. Imports of Chinese goods face tariffs now, but most brands have not invested in domestic capacity; instead they are cutting Chinese orders and shifting to other Asian countries, which means zero impact on US domestic manufacturing jobs or revenue.
major_players: Nike (footwear, apparel; limited domestic manufacturing)
Adidas (partial automation in Atlanta, but 97% production overseas)
Under Armour (footwear; exploring Baltimore factory)
Spalding (basketballs, owned by Spalding Sports Worldwide)
Callaway Golf
Ping (golf clubs; custom manufacturing)
Easton Sports (baseball bats, protective gear)
Rawlings (baseball gloves, equipment)
outlook: The next 12-24 months will determine whether tariffs remain the industry's defining constraint or whether supply-chain diversification stabilizes costs. If tariffs hold above 30% on Chinese goods, most brands will have completed their shift to Vietnam, India, and Indonesia by late 2026, but US domestic manufacturers will see zero benefit because capacity will not move to America. Domestic manufacturers will continue consolidating and specializing in high-margin niche and custom products, especially as direct-to-retailer channels expand. Participation-driven growth (golf, pickleball, youth sports) will keep wholesale demand healthy, but that does not translate to domestic manufacturing jobs or revenue growth. The real wildcard is whether the Trump administration escalates tariffs further or negotiates relief by mid-2026. A 40%+ tariff regime would force more brands to onshore, but current evidence (Nike's failed Mexico factory) shows that automation does not fully replace labor, and US wage costs are incompatible with commodity sporting goods. Most likely scenario: domestic manufacturing stays flat or declines slowly, imports shift from China to lower-tariff countries, prices rise for consumers, retail consolidates further, and niche/custom manufacturers thrive while commodity producers exit.

title: US Athletic Event Organizers Industry 2025-2026
one_liner: Running and obstacle course races are booming as health-conscious adults prioritize fitness and social connection, driving double-digit growth despite rising entry fees and labor costs.
one_sentence: The US Athletic Event Organizers industry is in multi-year growth (5.9% in 2026) driven by health consciousness, running club booms, and strong corporate wellness spending, with market consolidation and digital platforms reshaping competition.
overview: The US Athletic Event Organizers industry, which runs marathons, 5Ks, cycling races, obstacle courses, and walking events without fixed facilities, is in a robust recovery and growth phase after the COVID-19 collapse. Revenue has reached $4.8 billion in 2026 (up from $3.1 billion in 2024), with races growing an average of 5.9% in the first half of 2026. Running club membership surged 59% globally and 25% in the US in recent years, while obstacle course racing alone is a $5.5 billion North American market projected to grow 8.2% annually through 2034. US marathon participation hit 432,562 runners in 2024, up 5%, with younger participants (under 25) growing from 9.2% of finishers in 2016 to 12.1% in 2024. The industry is being reshaped by market consolidation (Spartan Race acquired Tough Mudder in 2025), the rise of digital registration platforms, and increasingly hybrid and virtual events.

key_stats.concentration: Low; Spartan Race (now including Tough Mudder US) is largest with 5.2 million participants globally 2025. Highly fragmented among small local organizers.
key_stats.businesses: Approximately 1,700 establishments (2026 estimate); dominated by private event companies and nonprofit organizers.

current_dynamics: Registration revenue is growing faster than participation: per-race revenue jumped 9.9% in 2026 while participation rose 5.9%, signaling organizers' growing pricing power as demand outpaces supply. Large races (5,000+ runners) recovered significantly and now grow 8.2% annually, faster than smaller cohorts, reversing years of post-COVID stagnation. Labor and operating costs are squeezing margins, with 71% of event planners expecting per-attendee costs to rise in 2026 due to staffing, insurance, permits, and venue expenses; marathon entry fees have climbed 5.3% year-over-year on average (Boston $250, Chicago $250-260, Tokyo $230 for US runners in 2026). Corporate wellness spending remains robust despite modest employee engagement (32% active participation), with 45% of organizations planning to increase wellness budgets in 2024-2025. Spartan Race's consolidation of Tough Mudder (2025) signals a shift toward vertical integration and brand portfolio strategies in a previously fragmented market.
major_players: Spartan Race (now includes Tough Mudder US; 5.2 million participants globally 2025)
Tough Mudder (UK, Canada, Germany under Spartan option agreements as of 2025)
Color Run (nontraditional themed running events)
RunSignup (dominant digital registration platform)
Race Roster, RedPodium, Run The Day (registration/timing platforms)
Local independent marathon and 5K organizers
Running USA (nonprofit industry association)
whats_growing: Running and trail running events account for 35.7% of industry revenue (2020). Obstacle course racing (OCR) is fastest-growing segment with 8.2% annual CAGR through 2034, driven by hybrid fitness/adventure appeal and corporate team participation. Large races (5,000+) now grow 8.2% annually after years of stagnation. Hybrid and virtual events are permanent: organizers use RunSignup and Race Roster for concurrent in-person and remote participation. Corporate wellness events remain strong, with 45% of companies planning budget increases and CEO ROI claims at 82% positive. Running club participation jumped 25% in the US in five years. Younger participants (under 25) grew from 9.2% to 12.1% of marathon finishers (2016-2024).
whats_shrinking: Multi-activity events (triathlons, biathlons) shrank to just 4.4% of industry revenue (2020) due to higher barrier to entry and difficulty converting to virtual formats. Cycling events declined from a higher share to 16.7% of revenue as running and obstacle races captured share. Youth sports participation in individual events (6-12 age group) fell from 50.8% in 2015 to 48.2% in 2018, reflecting rising travel league costs. First-time marathon finishers as a proportion of overall runners are declining; repeat participation is weak, with only 12.8% of 2024 marathoners returning in 2025. Overall leisure time spent on sports remains stagnant (5.3 hours daily in 2020, projected 0.4% annual growth through 2025).
recent_developments: August 2025: Spartan Race completes acquisition of Tough Mudder US after years of consolidation strategy; Spartan now operates 500+ annual US events and 5.2 million global participants.

February 2026: RunSignup releases 2025 Race Trends Report showing per-race revenue up 9.9% while participation grew 5%, signaling pricing power and add-on sales (merchandise, premium bibs) as key revenue levers.
Mid-2026: RunSignup reports races grew 5.9% in first half of 2026; large races (5,000+) grew 8.2%, fastest cohort growth, indicating market maturation and organizer professionalization.
2025-2026: HYROX (indoor fitness racing hybrid format) explodes: 750,000+ athletes in 2025 (100% growth YoY), affiliate gym network triples from 2,500 to 8,500 partner locations in 12 months.
2025-2026: Digital registration platforms now standard; virtual and hybrid race options become permanent; organizers no longer view remote participation as pandemic-only.
June 2025: SFIA reports 250 million Americans participated in at least one sport, fitness, or leisure activity (first time); running/jogging leads growth among younger groups.
themes: Social and community connection (running clubs, group fitness)
Digital transformation and virtual/hybrid event adoption
Labor cost inflation and margin pressure
Gen Z and younger participant engagement
outlook: Revenue is projected to grow 5-7% annually through 2026-2027 as health consciousness and corporate wellness spending remain robust. Running and obstacle course segments will lead, with OCR's 8.2% CAGR suggesting it could become the industry's fastest-growing category. Pricing power will persist due to strong demand, but entry fee resistance may emerge if growth slows or macro conditions weaken. Market consolidation will likely accelerate: Spartan's Tough Mudder acquisition signals a shift toward multiformat portfolios and centralized platforms, potentially squeezing small independent organizers. Virtual and hybrid race adoption will stabilize as a permanent 10-15% of market, providing year-round revenue options. Labor cost inflation remains a headwind, with organizers pressured to invest more in staffing, permits, insurance, and safety compliance. Corporate participation will remain strong as companies seek measurable wellness ROI and team-building, though passive employee engagement (32% active rate) will limit organic growth. Competition from gyms, home fitness, and digital fitness apps will intensify as subscription fitness (Peloton, HYROX affiliates) offer convenience; however, the social and experiential nature of live events provides differentiation that remote fitness cannot replicate.
how_it_makes_money: Event organizers earn revenue from three primary streams. Registration and entry fees (the largest source) now average $104.74 per marathon nationally (2026, up 5.3% YoY) with smaller races (5Ks) at lower prices. Sponsorships and partnerships (apparel brands, sports drinks, fitness companies, local businesses) cover significant event costs and are pitched to brands as high-profile, audience-rich marketing opportunities. Add-on and ancillary revenue (merchandise, food/beverage, premium bibs, timing chips, photos, coaching clinics) grew faster than base registration in 2026 (9.9% vs. 5.9% participation growth), signaling organizers' shift to upselling. Nonprofit organizers also fundraise for charitable causes (walk-for-cancer events). Virtual and hybrid events now open year-round revenue by removing geographic and seasonal barriers: RunSignup and similar platforms take a small per-registration fee (typically $0.50-$1.50 plus processing) and provide the full race logistics stack.
cost_structure: Labor (staffing, race directors, course marshals, volunteers) is the largest controllable cost, exacerbated by rising wage pressures; 71% of planners cite labor as driving budget increases in 2025-2026. Permits and municipal fees are mandatory and growing (every city requires proof of liability insurance and additional insured status). Insurance (general liability, event cancellation, medical coverage) ranges $2,500-$5,000 for mid-size events. Venue and logistics (course setup, timing systems, sound, signage, portable restrooms, water stations) consume 20-35% of budgets depending on race size. Marketing (digital ads, email, social media, partnerships) is necessary to drive registration; platforms like RunSignup have shifted organizers from media buys to commission-based acquisition models. Technology (timing, registration, results platforms) is increasingly outsourced to SaaS providers. Materials, printing, and participant merchandise add incremental costs. Fixed costs mean larger events have better economies of scale, while small local races operate on thin margins (often 5-10%).

title: US Auto Extended Warranty Providers
one_liner: A $32.7–$38.7 billion market (2025–2026) selling protection plans on used and new cars, driven by aging vehicles but squeezed by digital disruption, regulatory scrutiny, and consolidation.
overview: The US auto extended warranty market sits in mature stagnation: revenue was $32.7 billion in 2025 growing at just 1.4%, climbing to roughly $38.7 billion in 2026 at a CAGR of 6–7% depending on the analyst. The industry is split three ways — car manufacturers, dealers, and third-party providers — but third-party players face structural headwinds. The average car on the road is now 12.6 years old (2025), creating demand for coverage after factory warranties expire, yet new car sales are soft, electric vehicles are entering the market with different warranty profiles, and the FTC is actively prosecuting fraud and right-to-repair violations. Digital sales (34.7% of U.S. transactions in 2025) are reshaping the sales mix, while AI-driven pricing and telematics are forcing providers to compete on risk models, not just price cuts.

key_stats.businesses: 404 firms as of 2025, growing 0.1% per year (indicates consolidation)
key_stats.concentration: Moderate-to-high; Assurant Solutions is dominant player; top players include Ally Financial, Chubb, Toyota Financial Services, Ford Motor Company, Zurich Insurance Group

current_dynamics: The industry is caught between two opposing forces. Aging vehicles keep demand alive — as the average fleet age hits 12.6 years, used-car warranty sales now outnumber new-car sales at a 3.2:1 ratio (2025). Yet new car sales remain sluggish in 2025–2026, shrinking the entry point for manufacturer and dealer warranties. Third-party providers face a trust deficit: the FTC refunded $449,000 to victims of American Vehicle Protection's telemarketing scams (October 2024), sued CarShield for $10 million (July 2024), and is suing Endurance Warranty Services (March 2025). Meanwhile, digital channels (now 34.7% of U.S. sales) are shifting the sales model away from dealer point-of-sale, and AI pricing engines that use telematics data are fragmenting the traditional price-cutting playbook. Consolidation marches on — the number of firms grew 0.1% annually 2020–2025 — but M&A was muted in 2025–2026 relative to prior years (iA Financial Group bought Global Warranty in February 2025 to gain Canada scale). Assurant, the dominant player, launched Vehicle Care Technology Plus in March 2025 (bundling car coverage with smartphone repair) to deepen lifetime customer value. Overall, the sector is flat-lined by new-car headwinds, held up by old cars, and destabilized by fraud, regulation, and digital disruption.
one_sentence: A saturated insurance sector where aging vehicles prop up revenues, but new-car sales slumps, digital disruption, FTC enforcement, and AI-driven pricing are grinding margins and forcing consolidation.
whats_growing: Used-vehicle warranty sales (3.2:1 ratio vs. new, 2025). Digital sales channels (34.7% of U.S. transactions, 2025). EV-specific warranty demand (as EV battery replacements cost thousands). AI-driven claims adjudication and telematics-based pricing. Assurant's Global Automotive segment (1% revenue growth 9M 2024; Vehicle Care bundling). Coverage for advanced tech (ADAS, connected-car systems).
whats_shrinking: New car extended warranties (sales constrained by sluggish new-car purchases, 2025). Third-party provider trust (due to FTC enforcement actions and fraud scandals). Dealer point-of-sale warranty sales (shifting to digital channels). Traditional labor-intensive claim processing (being displaced by AI).
recent_developments: October 2024: FTC refunds $449,000 to 18,255 consumers harmed by American Vehicle Protection Corp. telemarketing scam.
July 2024: FTC settles $10 million case against CarShield for deceptive warranty claims.
March 2025: Assurant launches Vehicle Care Technology Plus, bundling car service contracts with smartphone repair benefits.
February 2025: iA Financial Group acquires Global Warranty to deepen Canadian used-vehicle segment reach.
March 2025: FeganScott files class-action lawsuit against Endurance Warranty Services on behalf of defrauded consumers.
June 2025: Victor Insurance unveils global extended warranty offering for OEMs and insurers.
outlook: The market will grow modestly at 6–7% CAGR through 2030 (reaching ~$47–$48 billion), but profitability will face headwinds. New-car sales remain the biggest constraint; if new-vehicle purchases stay soft in 2026–2027, growth may stall. EV adoption will reshape warranty demand — EVs come with longer factory coverage (8 years/100k miles standard in 2025), and used-EV buyers may trade new extended warranties for battery health assurance rather than bumper-to-bumper plans. Consolidation will accelerate as smaller third-party players either merge for scale or exit; trust deficits make brand and reputation critical. Regulation (FTC right-to-repair, state capital-adequacy rules) will tighten, raising compliance costs. AI pricing and digital distribution will become table-stakes, meaning providers who don't invest in claims automation and telematics-linked underwriting will lose to larger competitors. The industry will likely bifurcate: major players (Assurant, Ally, OEM-backed insurers) bundling warranties into lifetime-value plays, and specialty providers focusing on niche risk pools (EV batteries, ADAS claims).
themes: Aging vehicles sustain demand but constrain growth
Digital disruption reshapes sales mix and pricing
Fraud and regulatory enforcement erode trust in third-party players
Consolidation driven by margin pressure and scale economics
AI and telematics fragment the price-war dynamic
EV transition tilts warranty risk profiles upward

title: US Auto Leasing, Loans & Sales Financing
one_liner: The $173.8B auto financing industry is contracting in 2026 as affordability collapses, subprime delinquencies hit record highs, EV lease returns trigger depreciation shocks, and tariffs push monthly payments over $750.
overview: The auto financing industry is in a stress state heading into late 2026. Market size has declined 2.0% in 2026 to $173.8B after years of growth, a sharp reversal from the 2.9% annual expansion the 2022 IBISWorld report projected. The core problem is affordability. Average new-car payments now exceed $750/month, used-car payments $540/month, and new-vehicle registrations fell 6% year-over-year while the used market stalled flat. Subprime borrowers face a credit crunch: delinquencies hit record 6.6% in January 2025, and 90-day-or-more rates reached 5.6% by Q1 2026. Lenders are bracing for the 300,000+ electric vehicles pouring off lease in 2026 after their residual values collapsed from 90% retention in 2022 to just 40% by late 2025, a $10B-plus loss cascade that is reshaping lease pricing and captive-finance confidence.

key_stats.businesses: ~4,000 establishments; 2,331 enterprises (2026 projection from 2022 data)
key_stats.employees: ~95,000 estimated (2026 extrapolation from 2022 baseline of 88,855 with 1.6% projected growth)
key_stats.concentration: High; Toyota Financial Services leads outstandings (~$1.78T across top 100 lenders), followed by GM Financial, Ally Financial; captive lenders (OEM-owned) dominate
key_stats.profit_margin: Estimated 27-28% (2026); margin compression from higher delinquencies and reserve builds
key_stats.originations: 12.7M loans in H1 2025 ($381B funded); Q1 2026 originations +1% YoY but decelerating

current_dynamics: The industry is caught in a three-way squeeze that is eroding traditional business models. First, monthly payments have become unaffordable for middle-income buyers. New-car payments average $750+/month (vs. $600-650 in 2022), driven by tariffs (vehicles up $3,000-$10,000), higher interest rates (6.39% average for new cars in Q1 2026 vs. historic lows in 2022), and longer loan terms (84-96 month loans now common). This affordability wall is killing originations: new-vehicle registrations fell 6% YoY, and used-car registrations were flat despite higher inventory. Second, credit quality is deteriorating fast. Subprime delinquencies hit a 31-year high of 6.6% in January 2025, and 90+ day delinquencies reached 5.6% by Q1 2026, driving repossession levels toward 3 million vehicles in 2025 (matching the Great Recession era). Lenders are tightening: subprime originations fell despite the volume, and the largest subprime lenders and used-car dealers are filing for bankruptcy (Tricolor Holdings liquidated in October 2025 amid fraud allegations; the sector is consolidating under distress). Third, EV leasing is imploding. Over 300,000 electric vehicles are returning to market in 2026 after their residual values crashed from 90% retention in 2022 to 40% by late 2025. This $10B+ loss is forcing captive lenders to reprrice down-lease deals and carry massive residual-value losses, upending the economics of lease-to-own chains. Regulatory pressure is mounting: the CFPB is tightening collections practices and data accuracy oversight, and new personal financial data-rights rules take effect through 2026-2030.
one_sentence:
Affordability collapse, record subprime delinquencies, and cascading EV lease depreciation are shrinking the US auto financing market in 2026 as lenders face a perfect storm of payment shocks, tariff pressures, and credit stress.</sentence>
<parameter name="whats_growing">EV financing innovation (performance-based loan structures; fintech peer-to-peer and crowdfunding platforms) is gaining traction, though from a tiny base. Used-car inventory levels are up 5% YoY, creating minor tailwinds for used-car financing volume. Prime-tier originations (credit score 720+) remain relatively resilient: $99.4B originated in Q1 2026 vs. $82.6B for all subprime/prime tiers, signaling a bifurcation toward affluent borrowers. Lease originations for top-tier lenders like Ally are holding up (up 28.6% YoY), suggesting captive and prime-focused operators are protecting share.
whats_shrinking:
Subprime originations are collapsing as delinquency rates hit 31-year highs and lender appetite evaporates. New-vehicle sales fell 6% YoY, driving new-car loan demand down. Used-car prices are stabilizing (no longer rising, as chip/supply crises abated) after the post-2022 boom, meaning financing amounts per vehicle are flat or declining. EV depreciation is cratering lease returns, forcing a $3,800+ cost per car into the dealer/captive finance chain via price increases, fewer incentives, and delivery charge hikes. Subprime lender headcount is shrinking via bankruptcy (First Brands, Tricolor in 2025) and consolidation.</shrinking>

September 2025: Atlanticus Holdings acquired Mercury Financial LLC, a fintech credit-card platform, to scale consumer credit offerings and diversify beyond auto.
Q1 2026: Auto loan originations +1% YoY but decelerating hard; subprime originations down; new-vehicle registrations -6% YoY; 90+ day delinquencies reached 5.6% (highest on record).
Late 2025: Average EV residual value collapsed to 40% of purchase price (from 90% in 2022), triggering $10B+ loss cascade for captive lenders and forcing repricing of lease portfolios.
January 2026: Federal tariffs on imported vehicles and parts began flowing through to new-car prices (+$3,000 to $10,000 MSRP), driving monthly payments over $750 and crushing affordability.
June 2026: CFPB advanced notice of proposed rulemaking to lower the 'larger nonbank' threshold from 10,000 to 1,050,000 annual originations, expanding regulatory oversight into fintech lenders.
themes: Affordability crisis — monthly payments exceed buyer capacity
Subprime distress — delinquencies at 31-year highs; bankruptcies spreading
EV residual-value shock — depreciation upending lease economics
Tariff pass-through — vehicle costs up $3K-$10K, compressing demand
Regulatory tightening — CFPB data rights, collections oversight, fair lending
Bifurcation by credit tier — prime resilient, subprime collapsing
outlook:
The industry will likely contract further through late 2026 and into 2027. Originations will remain soft as affordability stays under pressure and tariff costs stick. Subprime consolidation will accelerate: weaker lenders will exit or merge; Atlanticus, some captive lenders, and large banks will gain share. EV lease returns will create a two-year repricing and depreciation-management crisis for captive finance arms, forcing stricter residual-value assumptions and lower lease-to-retail pipelines. Regulatory pressure will persist, raising compliance costs for smaller players. Used-car financing will hold steadier than new-car financing because prices are stabilizing and inventory is rising, improving buyer options. The prime-tier bifurcation (affluent borrowers insulated from payment shocks via higher income) will deepen, leaving subprime and near-prime borrowers shut out of credit. If interest rates fall materially in late 2026 or 2027, some demand could return; if they hold or rise further, expect 2-3 more years of single-digit growth or contraction. Total market size is unlikely to recover to the 2022 baseline within 18 months.</outlook>

title: US Auto Mechanics Industry 2025-2026
one_liner: A mature, consolidating repair-and-maintenance market split between independent shops gaining share and dealerships losing customers to price pressure and wait times, shaped by an aging fleet, EV complexity, technician shortages, and right-to-repair regulation opening data access.
overview: The US auto mechanics industry is a $92.1 billion market in 2026, operating near flat (−0.1% growth in 2026 after 1.2% five-year CAGR through 2026). Independent repair shops have captured 38% of market share as of 2025, up from 32% a year earlier, while dealership service slipped from 47% to 42%—despite dealerships recording all-time service revenue of $9.23 million per location on average. The industry is caught between structural tailwinds (an aging fleet now averaging 12.8 years, aging vehicles needing more repairs) and headwinds (fewer miles per vehicle, technician shortages costing shops $500K+ annually, parts inflation, tariff uncertainty, and rising diagnostic equipment costs). Consolidation by private equity is accelerating: 14 PE-backed platforms are actively acquiring independent shops, the "Big 5" collision-repair consolidators now operate 4,019 locations (13.3% of shop share, 31.7% of revenue), and Mavis acquired ~1,200 Midas locations in 2025. Electric vehicles are reshaping the skill profile—EV repairs grew from 24.80 billion in 2025 to 29.82 billion in 2026 market size, with diagnostics and high-voltage work now table stakes.

key_stats.businesses: 282,637 establishments (2022 baseline); highly fragmented with ~67% nonemployer shops
key_stats.employees: 614,433 (2022 baseline); technician shortage leaves ~67,000 positions unfilled at end of 2025
key_stats.profit_margin: 6.30% (2022 baseline); pressure from rising labor and parts costs
key_stats.concentration: Low (highly fragmented); but consolidation accelerating—Big 5 collision repairers at 31.7% of revenue

current_dynamics: Dealership service departments are hemorrhaging customers despite record absolute revenue: only 29% of vehicle owners now service at the dealership where they bought (down from 33%), and 54% of owners of cars two years old or newer return to the selling dealership (down from 72% in 2023). Independent shops are scaling faster—38% market share in 2025 vs. 32% one year prior—by offering lower overhead, shorter wait times, and faster turnaround when dealerships lack technician staff. The industry is trapped between two forces: aging vehicles (12.8 years average, the 4–11-year-old cohort near all-time high post-warranty) drive repair demand, but each vehicle is being driven ~400 fewer miles per year than in 2019, and repair frequency (cars being serviced) continues to shrink despite record total miles. Technician shortages are acute and structural: ~67,000 open positions remained unfilled at year-end 2025, with retiring Baby Boomers set to open 100,000 more by 2029; average technician hourly pay stands at $26.18 (2025), a 2.3% annual rise that shop operators struggle to absorb. Diagnostic and ADAS equipment costs are forcing consolidation upward—shops now need $5,000–$50,000+ for modern diagnostic tools plus $300–$1,500 annual update subscriptions, and ADAS calibration frames run $3,000–$8,000, creating a capital barrier that weeds out small players. Tariffs, parts inflation, and supply chain disruptions remain top concerns (46% of shops cite parts affordability, 45% cite supply chain disruption); shops absorb cost increases rather than passing them fully to increasingly price-conscious customers. Right-to-repair momentum is reshaping competitive dynamics: Massachusetts and Maine now mandate OEM data sharing, 33+ state bills pending in early 2026, and a federal law is gaining congressional attention—opening diagnostic access to independent shops and threatening dealership service lock-in.
one_sentence: A mature, consolidating repair market where independent shops are taking share from dealerships via speed and price, while struggling to hire enough skilled technicians, invest in EV diagnostics, and navigate tariffs and parts inflation.
whats_growing: Independent repair shop market share (38% in 2025 vs. 32% in 2024); EV repair and diagnostic services (market grew to $29.82 billion in 2026 from $24.80 billion in 2025, 20.3% CAGR projected 2026–2031); private equity consolidation platforms (5 new PE entrants in H1 2025 alone, $5B+ of equity deployed into auto repair platforms since 2021); technician wage pressure (2.3% CAGR); older vehicle fleet repairs (average fleet age 12.8 years, highest post-warranty cohort on record).
whats_shrinking: Dealership service market share (from 47% in 2024 to 42% in 2025, continuing decline in 2026); vehicles being serviced (despite record total miles traveled, repair frequency and total-loss frequency climbing to 22–23% of insurance claims); miles per vehicle year-over-year (2025 average ~400 miles below 2019 baseline, projections for 2026 flat or down slightly); shop labor hours per vehicle (EV adoption reducing routine maintenance need despite higher diagnostic/calibration load).
recent_developments: Mavis Tire Express acquired ~1,200 Midas locations in 2025, consolidating one of the largest independent service platforms
5 new private equity entrants into collision repair consolidation in H1 2025; 14 PE-backed platforms now actively acquiring; Big 5 consolidators operate 4,019 locations (31.7% of revenue share)
Massachusetts and Maine right-to-repair laws began requiring OEM data sharing in 2025; 33+ new state bills introduced in early 2026; federal legislation gaining momentum
EV repair service market reached $29.82 billion in 2026, up from $24.80 billion in 2025 (20.3% CAGR through 2031); one in four new cars sold worldwide is now electric
Independent shops captured 38% market share by 2025 (up from 32% year prior) as dealership service dropped to 42% market share; only 29% of vehicle owners now service at selling dealership
Tariff uncertainty and parts inflation (46% of shops report parts affordability as top concern in 2026; 45% cite supply chain disruption as persistent challenge)
outlook: The industry is likely to grow modestly over 2026–2031, driven by an aging fleet and EV adoption, but with significant structural headwinds. Market size is projected to remain flat to slightly negative in 2026 (−0.1%), then recover to ~1.3–1.9% annualized growth through 2027 and beyond as vehicle miles stabilize and EV service demand ramps. Consolidation by PE will intensify, particularly in collision repair and multi-location chains, squeezing independent shops without scale or capital for diagnostic tools. Dealership service will continue to lose share to independent operators, though absolute dealership revenue may hold steady or grow due to higher ticket values from EV diagnostics and ADAS calibration. The technician shortage will remain acute through 2029—100,000+ open positions from Baby Boomer retirements—forcing wage growth and pushing shops to invest in technician training partnerships and apprenticeship programs to compete. Right-to-repair legislation will accelerate in 2026, gradually eroding dealership service lock-in and allowing independent shops with proper tooling and training to capture more out-of-warranty and high-mileage work. Tariff and parts inflation dynamics remain a wildcard; if tariffs persist, repair costs will climb faster than labor rates, potentially suppressing demand among price-sensitive consumers and narrowing margins across the board. Shops that survive the next five years will be those that (1) invest heavily in EV diagnostics and technician upskilling, (2) adopt subscription software platforms for workflow and inventory, and (3) either consolidate or form referral networks to share diagnostic equipment costs and build economies of scale.

how_it_makes_money: Revenue comes from labor (charged at $100–$139 per hour on average, higher at dealerships; technician compensation $26.18/hour average), parts markup (50–100% typical margin), and diagnostic fees. Shops perform scheduled preventative maintenance (31% of revenue), powertrain repair (18.1%), brake repair (17.4%), electrical/ADAS work (6.4%), and miscellaneous (muffler, heating, alignment). Commercial fleets (delivery, commercial vehicles) are the second-largest market segment after consumers. Revenue per employee is high (a strength of the industry), but profit margins (6.3% in 2022, compressed since) are squeezed by technician wages, parts costs, and diagnostic equipment capital outlays. title: US Auto Parts Remanufacturing Industry: Current State 2025-2026
one_liner: A mature, consolidating industry being reshaped by tariffs, battery-scale electrification, and major bankruptcies, yet enjoying counter-cyclical resilience and regulatory tailwinds around circular-economy mandates.
overview: The US auto parts remanufacturing industry is in flux as of mid-2026. The market remains substantial—valued at roughly $63-69 billion globally in 2024-2025, with North America holding about 32-35% of the global market. However, the sector faces acute stress: First Brands Group (which owned Cardone, the largest remanufacturer in North America) filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy in September 2025 with $9.3 billion in obligations, triggering widespread layoffs and supply disruptions. Simultaneously, 25% tariffs on auto parts (effective April 2025) have compressed margins and forced operators to localize sourcing. Yet tailwinds remain: aging US vehicle fleets, regulatory mandates for circular-economy practices, and the emerging opportunity in EV battery recovery (a $2.1 billion market in 2025, projected to hit $12.8 billion by 2034) are creating new revenue streams and attracting capital and OEM engagement.

key_stats.employees: ~11,000 in US (2021 baseline); multiple thousands displaced via bankruptcies (2025)
key_stats.businesses: Estimated 80-100 establishments in US; major consolidation ongoing; Cardone once largest remanufacturer, now in bankruptcy restructuring
key_stats.concentration: Moderate to high; Cardone (via First Brands), Robert Bosch, ZF Friedrichshafen, Valeo, and Denso dominate; North America = 32-35% of global market
key_stats.profit_margin: 7.2-7.7% (2021-2026 forecast from 2022 report); compressed by 2025 tariffs

current_dynamics: The industry is experiencing a major inflection point around electrification and tariffs. Traditional engine and transmission remanufacturing (which comprised 27% of revenue in 2021) still dominates, but EV powertrains—particularly high-voltage batteries and electric motors—are emerging as the highest-growth segment, with 21.8% annual growth projected. The 25% tariff on auto parts (April 2025) triggered immediate margin compression and a pivot toward domestic sourcing; import volumes fell 10% year-over-year in 2025, but North American suppliers gained share relative to Europe and Asia. The First Brands bankruptcy shocked the market: Cardone, which had built a reputation as the largest independent remanufacturer offering parts at 50% discounts to new, suddenly faced reorganization, liquidation pressures, and job cuts (1,200+ jobs eliminated). Simultaneously, environmental regulations and OEM circular-economy commitments are creating tailwinds: remanufacturing reduces energy use by 85% compared to new manufacturing, regulators are phasing in recycled-content targets (EU examples: 15% in six years, 25% in ten), and leading automakers (Ford, GM, Stellantis) are embedding reman into long-term supply strategies. The vehicle fleet continues aging (average vehicle age trending upward), sustaining demand for repair-oriented remanufactured parts even as new-vehicle prices rise.
one_sentence: A maturing, tariff-hit sector pivoting from traditional parts to EV batteries and circular-economy models, roiled by bankruptcies but supported by aging fleets, regulatory mandates, and OEM engagement.
whats_growing: EV battery and high-voltage component remanufacturing (36.5% surge in demand for EV drive systems and controllers; EV HV component segment at 21.8% CAGR through 2034); battery second-life and stationary energy-storage applications; digital diagnostics and AI-driven process optimization; OEM-embedded remanufacturing programs; demand from supply-chain resilience seekers post-COVID/post-semiconductor-crisis.
whats_shrinking: Traditional mechanical-parts remanufacturing (starters, alternators, steering) due to EV adoption and parts simplification; headcount and number of establishments (long-term structural decline, accelerated by bankruptcies and offshoring); profit margins (tariff compression in 2025); import competition vulnerability (tariffs shifted incentives toward domestic reman).
recent_developments: September 2025: First Brands Group filed Chapter 11 bankruptcy with $9.3 billion in obligations; Cardone (largest North American remanufacturer) entered restructuring; alleged $2.3 billion factoring fraud; 1,200+ job cuts across Ohio and other facilities (Distribution Strategy Group, May 2026).

April 2025: 25% US tariff on auto parts components and powertrain products went into effect; import volumes fell 10% YoY; North American suppliers' market share rose from 41% to 44% of US imports (Morgan Lewis, October 2025).
2025: EV high-voltage component remanufacturing market valued at $2.1 billion; projected to reach $12.8 billion by 2034, 21.8% CAGR (multiple sources).

Q3-Q4 2025: Supply-chain disruption from First Brands collapse rippled through distributor networks; inventory liquidation and fragmented contracts pressured smaller remanufacturers (Distribution Strategy Group, 2026).

2026: Leading automakers (Ford, GM, Stellantis) expanded in-house and partnership remanufacturing programs; battery-repurposing second-life initiatives launched; EU regulatory trajectory (15% recycled-content target in 6 years; December 2025 provisional agreement).

2024-2026: Tariffs, supply-chain localization, and digitalization shifted industry focus toward regional hubs, IoT-enabled predictive maintenance, and data-driven inventory management; battery-extraction and recycling startups attracted venture capital.
major_players: Cardone Industries (now under First Brands Group restructuring; largest North American remanufacturer prior to bankruptcy)
Robert Bosch GmbH (global leader; engine, transmission, electronics remanufacturing)
ZF Friedrichshafen AG (transmission, powertrain, safety systems reman)
Denso Corporation (electrical, powertrain, thermal components)
Valeo SA (electrical, thermal, powertrain systems)
Meritor Inc. (commercial vehicle drivetrain components)
Ford, General Motors, Stellantis (increasing in-house OEM reman programs)
Budweg Caliper A/S (brakes and suspension systems)
Raybestos (brake systems; First Brands portfolio, now in transition)
outlook: The outlook for 2026-2027 is mixed but trending upward for niche, technology-forward operators and downward for commodity remanufacturers exposed to tariffs and traditional-parts decline. Market growth is expected to accelerate to 7-8% annually as EV reman (batteries, motors, power electronics, thermal systems) becomes mainstream; OEM engagement and regulatory mandates will sustain demand and margin pressure on commodity segments will ease somewhat if tariff relief or stabilization occurs. Consolidation will continue: smaller, undercapitalized shops will either fail or merge into larger regional players or OEM-owned operations. The Cardone bankruptcy may ultimately prove a catalyst—as bankruptcy-court sales and restructuring play out through 2026, competitors may consolidate market share and gain access to Cardone's customer base at discount prices. Localization will persist: tariffs and supply-chain resilience concerns lock in domestic sourcing for at least 2-3 more years. Battery circular-economy policies (EU phased targets, US state EV mandates) will drive investment in battery extraction and second-life logistics. Profitability will stabilize at 7-8% for well-positioned players, but head count will continue its long decline (offshoring, automation, parts simplification). The most bullish scenario is that remanufacturing emerges as a strategic pillar of EV supply chains, with reman costs and environmental benefits creating a defensible moat against raw-materials price shocks and geopolitical supply-chain risk.
cost_structure: Labor: traditionally 30-35% of operating costs, declining due to offshoring and automation; Raw materials and cores: 40-50%, including steel, copper, and (newly) lithium and cobalt from EV batteries; Equipment and tooling: 10-15%, rising as operators invest in EV-component and battery-diagnostics capabilities; Overhead (facilities, logistics, inventory management): 10-15%.
how_it_makes_money: Sale of remanufactured parts at 50-75% of new-part prices to aftermarket retailers, wholesalers, auto parts stores, and increasingly to OEMs for warranty replacement and circular-economy programs. Margin compression from tariffs, commodity competition, and labor offsets pricing power in high-value segments (electrical, transmissions, EV batteries). Emerging revenue streams: battery second-life leasing/repurposing for grid storage, OEM supply agreements with guaranteed volumes, and contract remanufacturing services for large fleet operators.
themes: EV battery and high-voltage component reman as highest-growth segment
Major consolidation via bankruptcies and M&A (Cardone crisis symptom)
Regulatory circular-economy mandates (EU, state-level EV policies)
OEM strategic engagement and in-house reman programs

title: US Auto Parts Wholesaling 2025-2026
one_liner: A mature wholesale distribution industry connecting auto part manufacturers to retailers and OEMs, currently navigating electrification disruption, tariff-driven supply chain restructuring, and consolidation pressures on smaller players.
overview: The US auto parts wholesaling industry reached $262.9 billion in revenue in 2026, growing at just 0.9% annually since 2021. The sector operates through 16,581 businesses as of 2026, down from the peak in earlier years due to ongoing consolidation. Digital transformation is reshaping how smaller wholesalers access inventory and pricing. The industry faces a historic inflection point: EV sales in the US are expected to decline 15.5% year-over-year in 2026, while 25% tariffs on imported auto parts (enacted in April 2025) are forcing reshoring decisions and triggering a wave of bankruptcies and job losses among smaller Tier 2 and Tier 3 suppliers who lack the scale to absorb tariff costs.

key_stats.businesses: 16,581 companies (2026)
key_stats.profit_margin: 4.9% (2021 baseline)
key_stats.concentration: Low; Genuine Parts Co. leads but no single player dominates wholesaling

current_dynamics: The industry faces headwinds from the elimination of the $7,500 EV tax credit on September 30, 2025, which reduced US EV sales growth to 8.2% market share by 2026—down sharply from earlier momentum. Tariffs imposed in April 2025 (25% on auto parts imports) have created dual pressures: large manufacturers are nearshoring supply chains to Mexico and other USMCA partners, while smaller suppliers—especially family-owned Tier 2/3 operations—face existential risk. A 2025 survey found 70% of small suppliers expect layoffs or investment cuts if tariffs persist. First Brands Group (Raybestos, Cardone, Autolite, FRAM) filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy in September 2025 with $6 billion in debt; other failures include Bohai Trimet and Cooper Standard plant closures. Meanwhile, wholesalers are racing to digitize: e-commerce channels are growing at 6.5% annually, with online platforms allowing smaller retailers to bypass traditional wholesalers. Supply chain complexity has spiked—45% of businesses cite inventory management as their top risk since 2022, a metric that has worsened each year.
one_sentence: US auto parts wholesaling is a mature, slowly growing ($263B in 2026, +0.9% CAGR) distribution sector now convulsing under tariffs, EV transition losses, and digital channel pressure that favors large consolidators and threatens smaller regional players with bankruptcy.

baseline_2022.growth: -0.3% (2016-2021, five-year annualized decline including COVID impact)

how_it_makes_money: Wholesalers buy auto parts from manufacturers and component suppliers, then distribute them to three customer segments: automotive manufacturers (OEM channel, ~40% of revenue), retail auto parts stores (~35%), and independent service providers and body shops (~25%). Revenue is split across thermal systems (24.4%), powertrain systems (23.2%), electrical/electronic components (23.2%), and mobility systems (22.6%). Margins compress when input costs rise or when manufacturers shortcut wholesalers via direct sales; they expand when wholesalers add high-margin services like parts configuration, warehouse management, or technical support.
cost_structure: High fixed costs: regional distribution networks, warehouse footprints, and inventory carrying costs represent the largest expense categories. Labor costs (wages, benefits) grew at 1.4% annually through 2026 as wholesalers expanded operations to add digital logistics and technical support. Transportation and logistics costs spiked in 2025-2026 due to tariff-driven freight volatility and nearshoring pressures. Input costs (parts procurement from manufacturers) have risen due to EV transition R&D by suppliers and inflation in electronics components, compressing gross margins industry-wide.
major_players: Genuine Parts Company (largest US wholesaler; owns NAPA Auto Parts)
Robert Bosch GmbH (German-owned, 4.2% market share in 2021; forecast 2-5% sales growth in 2026)
Denso Corporation (third-largest, specializes in thermal systems)
Foreign-owned wholesalers (three of the four largest in 2021 were foreign-owned, combined 10.8% market share)
Note: Traditional retail chains like Advance Auto Parts closed 700+ stores in 2025 and are not pure wholesalers but affected the downstream demand
whats_growing: E-commerce and digital wholesale channels (+6.5% annually); demand for EV-specific components and advanced driver assistance systems (ADAS) parts; parts for older vehicles as fleet average age rises; nearshored supply chains and Mexico-based alternatives to Chinese suppliers; M&A activity (67 auto companies announced M&A by mid-2026, with parts suppliers forming the bulk of deals); technology-focused supplier acquisitions (semiconductors, sensors, software in over 50% of 2025 deals).
whats_shrinking: Demand for traditional internal combustion engine parts (exhaust, fuel systems, transmissions—absent in EVs); OEM-channel revenue (new car production weakness, with US EV sales declining 15.5% in 2026); wholesale businesses under 50 employees (bankruptcies and closures accelerating through 2026, especially among family-owned Tier 2/3 suppliers); retail auto parts store chains (Advance Auto Parts exit, predicted wave of bankruptcies in 2026 per analysts). Profitability under tariff pressure for importers; smaller suppliers' margins compressed by 25% tariffs with no offsetting pricing power.
recent_developments: April 3, 2025: Trump administration imposes 25% tariff on imported auto parts and vehicles; May 3, 2025 expansion to components under Section 232 (Trade Expansion Act). Motor & Equipment Manufacturers Association survey finds 70% of small suppliers expect layoffs or investment cuts if tariffs persist.
September 28, 2025: First Brands Group (Raybestos, Cardone, Autolite, FRAM) files Chapter 11 with $6B debt and $4B off-balance-sheet liabilities; eliminates 1,200+ jobs across four facility closures.
September 30, 2025: US eliminates $7,500 EV tax credit, disrupting EV market momentum and wholesale demand for EV-specific parts.

February 2026: Supreme Court rules 2025 tariffs under IEEPA unconstitutional; Trump administration signals intent to pursue tariffs under different legal authority, prolonging supply chain uncertainty.
Mid-2025 (complete by June 2026): Advance Auto Parts finalizes closure of 523 corporate stores and 204 independent locations; shuts four West Coast distribution centers.
June 12, 2026 (mid-year): 67 automotive companies announce M&A plans; parts suppliers dominate deal wave driven by margin pressures, tariff restructuring, and supply chain resilience needs.
themes: EV transition creating winners and losers
Digital wholesale channels and e-commerce bypass
Global supply chain redesign and nearshoring
outlook: The industry will remain sluggish through 2026-2027. Market growth is forecast at 0.9% CAGR, well below inflation, signaling mature-industry stagnation. Tariff policy remains the biggest wild card: if tariffs hold or escalate, 2026 bankruptcies will accelerate and smaller wholesalers will consolidate into larger networks or exit. EV penetration in the US is slowing due to credit elimination, but global EV parts demand (especially batteries, motors, sensors) is growing fast; wholesalers linked to international supply chains will outperform. Digital channels will continue cannibalizing traditional wholesale margins, favoring platforms like Amazon Business and manufacturer direct-to-retailer models. Consolidators with capital and scale (Genuine Parts, large PE-backed platforms) will acquire distressed assets and smaller regional players, further concentrating the market. The outlook is for 2-3 years of negative free cash flow among smaller players, a wave of Chapter 11 filings in 2026-2027, and eventual stabilization around a smaller, more concentrated industry (maybe 14,000-15,000 businesses by 2028).

title: US Automated Guided Vehicle Manufacturing Industry 2025–2026
one_liner: Shrinking domain overtaken by AMRs as tech commoditizes, yet AGV makers chase growth in healthcare and logistics while tariffs and labor shortages drive reshoring.
overview: The US AGV manufacturing industry is shifting underneath its feet. Traditionally tape-guided and laser-guided vehicles once dominated material handling, but autonomous mobile robots (AMRs)—smarter, more flexible, and cheaper to deploy—are eating into AGV sales across warehouses and factories. The industry is consolidating: smaller competitors are folding (Kivnon Logistica in Spain entered bankruptcy in late 2024; ek Robotics in Germany failed), while giants like JBT (which acquired Marel in January 2025) and Teradyne (which owns MiR and is opening a 67,000-sq.-ft. US headquarters in late 2026) are bulking up. Labor shortages remain acute—76% of supply chains report significant shortfalls—but instead of just buying AGVs, warehouses are now adopting faster-deploying AMRs. E-commerce still grows, but it no longer feels like a boom: Amazon, which now operates over a million robots itself, has partially closed its logistics to pure-play robotics vendors by launching Amazon Supply Chain Services (a 3PL offering) and developing proprietary automation.

key_stats.growth: 2.3% (2025), 4.1% CAGR past 5 years (2020–2025); forward outlook slowing vs. 2015–2021
key_stats.businesses: 72 companies (US, 2025)
key_stats.concentration: Moderate-to-high; JBT/Marel largest player, followed by Jervis B. Webb, Dematic

baseline_2022.growth: 14.8% CAGR (2016–2021, pandemic recovery; 5-year outlook 2021–2026 was 5.1% CAGR)

current_dynamics: The US AGV industry is no longer the shiny growth story of the 2010s. Global AGV-AMR markets have merged conceptually (AMRs are now $2.75B–$7.07B by 2032), and the gap is widening: AMRs employ SLAM-based navigation and AI to adapt to unmapped spaces in real time, while traditional AGVs require pre-installed tape or laser infrastructure and are slower to redeploy. New installations increasingly favor SLAM-based systems (50%+ by 2025); multi-mode AGVs (laser in high-precision zones, natural navigation elsewhere) are emerging as a bridge. Startups and mid-tier vendors are getting squeezed: Locus Robotics (USA, $109.7M revenue in 2025) and OTTO Motors (Canada) survive through venture funding, but smaller European peers (Kivnon, ek Robotics) are exiting. Meanwhile, blue-chip integrators and robotics arms (Teradyne, JBT, ABB before its 2025 SoftBank divestiture) are consolidating, signaling that the margin is in services, fleet management software, and downstream customer lock-in, not unit sales. Labor shortage severity (76% of supply chains impacted; 500k open US logistics jobs) continues to anchor demand, but adoption is not linear: only 10% of companies deploy automation effectively, while 34% remain in wait-and-see mode. Trade tariffs (US–China at 57.6% average in Sept 2025) are disrupting component costs and favor domestic assembly, potentially benefiting US manufacturers. E-commerce as a demand driver is plateauing: predicted growth slowed from 15.5% annually (pre-2021) to 8.1% projected (2021–2028).
one_sentence: AGV manufacturing in the US is a maturing, margin-pressured segment ceding ground to cheaper, smarter AMRs and facing consolidation, though labor shortages and tariff reshoring create near-term pockets of demand in healthcare and legacy logistics operations.
whats_growing: Healthcare logistics (JBT's ATLIS AGVs for hospitals); natural-navigation and vision-guided AGVs (SLAM-based, no tape required); fleet management software (projected $1.58B in 2025 → $5.23B by 2032, 17% CAGR); domestic manufacturing capacity (reshoring under tariff pressure); specialty vertical AGVs for ports and automotive assembly lines.
whats_shrinking: Tape-guided and magnetic-guided AGVs (being displaced by SLAM); price-sensitive commodity AGV segments (facing import competition and AMR displacement); small independent AGV makers (consolidation wave); new orders in generic warehouse material handling (Amazon Robotics and third-party AMR deployments now undercut traditional AGV economics).
recent_developments: January 2025: JBT Corporation completed acquisition of Marel and rebranded as JBT Marel, consolidating food-processing machinery and AGV divisions; Q2 2025 backlog reached $1.4 billion, suggesting sustained order flow despite market headwinds.
October 2025: ABB divested its Robotics division to SoftBank for $5.375 billion, exiting the direct-manufacturing space (though ABB had been a secondary player, this signals sector consolidation).
Late 2024: Kivnon Logistica (Spanish AGV maker) entered bankruptcy restructuring, citing automotive downturn ripple effects and slowed AGV demand.
By 2025: SLAM-based (natural navigation) AGVs captured over 50% of new installations, marking a decisive tech shift away from tape-guided systems; multi-mode hybrid AGVs emerging as compromise.

April 2025: Toyota Industries merged viastore's North American pallet-handling offerings with Bastian Solutions, consolidating automation integration capabilities and signaling the end of point-solution AGV vendors.

2025–2026: Teradyne announced opening a 67,000-sq.-ft. US headquarters (late 2026) in Michigan as HQ for MiR and Universal Robots, betting on US manufacturing reshoring; Teradyne expects large e-commerce customer to triple revenue contribution 2025→2026.
major_players: JBT Marel Corporation (largest US AGV player; ATLIS healthcare brand; acquired Marel Jan 2025)
Teradyne Robotics (owns MiR, world's leading AMR; expanding US ops 2026)
Jervis B. Webb Company (historic AGV specialist, now part of Daifuku)
Dematic Corporation (warehouse automation via conveyors and AGVs)
Amazon Robotics (proprietary fleet; now also offers third-party 3PL via Amazon Supply Chain Services)
Locus Robotics (warehouse AMRs, $109.7M revenue 2025, VC-backed)
OTTO Motors (heavy-duty industrial AMRs, Canada, $83M Series B 2025)
Geek+ (warehouse robotics leader in Asia and emerging markets)
Seegrid (vision-guided AGVs with natural navigation)
MiR (Mobile Industrial Robots, Denmark, 25,000+ units deployed globally; part of Teradyne)
themes: Commodity-to-SaaS shift: AGV hardware margin compression + fleet-management software becoming the profit center
Natural navigation / SLAM adoption: tape-free, AI-first systems displace traditional laser/magnetic AGVs
Consolidation & exit: smaller AGV makers bankrupt or acquired; blue chips (Teradyne, JBT, Toyota) roll up
AMR invasion: autonomous mobile robots (faster, cheaper to deploy, flexible) ceding 'pure AGV' into niche healthcare + precision manufacturing
Labor shortage anchor + adoption gap: severe shortage (76% of supply chains) drives demand, but only 10% execute automation well
E-commerce plateau & Amazon vertical integration: 15%+ growth era over; Amazon's 1M+ robots + ASCS 3PL reduce TAM for pure-play AGV vendors
cost_structure: Labor and engineering dominate (skilled design/integration for customized deployments). Materials cost low (commodity sensors, motors, control boards falling in price). Software development rising (fleet management, SLAM algorithms, cloud orchestration). Supply-chain costs volatile due to tariffs (Sept 2025: China imports at 57.6% avg tariff). Scale disadvantage for small makers (large orders from Teradyne, JBT, Amazon amortize R&D faster).
how_it_makes_money: Manufacturers generate revenue from direct system sales (units + installation), recurring software-as-a-service (fleet management, data analytics, dispatch optimization), maintenance and spare parts, and professional services (integration, training). Consolidators (JBT, Teradyne) generate additional margin from software, managed services, and customer lock-in. Startups rely on venture capital and unit sales until reaching SaaS scale.
outlook: The US AGV industry will grow 2–3% annually through 2026–2028 (vs. historical 14%+), ceding growth to AMRs which are forecast 14.4% CAGR. Tape and laser-guided AGVs will shrink as standard options; SLAM-based systems and custom healthcare/automotive AGVs will command higher prices and margins. Consolidation will accelerate—expect 2–3 more mid-tier exits, and JBT/Teradyne will likely acquire smaller specialists. E-commerce demand will plateau but remain steady due to fulfillment velocity expectations. Labor shortages will keep logistics automation spending elevated, but end-users will increasingly choose cheaper, faster-deploying AMRs over traditional AGVs. Healthcare (aging population, staffing crisis) and ports (container volumes) offer AGV tailwinds. Tariffs on Chinese robotics components will favor US assembly and reshoreable segments. Profitability will edge up (from 9.8% to 10–11%) as product mixes shift to software and services, but unit sales growth will remain sub-GDP.
